topics.title: Respiration, respiratory substrates and do plants breathe?

learn.hook: A banyan tree can be hundreds of years old and enormous, yet it has no lungs. How does every cell in it get oxygen?
points: Cellular respiration is the breaking of C–C bonds of complex compounds by oxidation within cells, releasing energy. The compounds oxidised are respiratory substrates: usually carbohydrates, but also proteins, fats and even organic acids in some plants.
Energy is not released in one step but in a series of slow, enzyme-controlled steps, and trapped as ATP, the energy currency of the cell.
Plants have no specialised respiratory organs; gas exchange occurs through stomata and lenticels.

Why plants manage without lungs: each part handles its own gas exchange; plants respire at far lower rates than animals; during photosynthesis O₂ is released inside the cells; living cells are close to the surface (in stems they lie in thin layers beneath the bark, with lenticels; interior cells are dead); loosely packed parenchyma gives a network of air spaces.

Complete combustion of glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (mostly heat). Cells instead oxidise glucose step by step. Some organisms are facultative or obligate anaerobes, and all organisms keep the machinery to partly oxidise glucose without O₂ (glycolysis), reflecting anaerobic ancestors.

example.q: In the combustion equation of glucose, how many molecules of O₂ are used per molecule of CO₂ released?

learn.reallife: Old trees along Indian roads have lenticels, tiny raised pores on their bark, that let air reach the living cells beneath.

learn.hook: Every organism on Earth, from bacteria to blue whales, runs glycolysis in its cytoplasm. It's the oldest energy app.
points: Glycolysis (Greek glycos = sugar, lysis = splitting) is the EMP pathway, worked out by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas. It occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms; in anaerobes it is the only respiratory process. It has ten enzyme-controlled reactions.
Glucose is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase (ATP used). This isomerises to fructose-6-phosphate, which is phosphorylated to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (second ATP used).
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate splits into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL).
PGAL is oxidised (two redox equivalents to NAD⁺, forming NADH + H⁺) and, with inorganic phosphate, becomes 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA).
ATP is made directly (substrate-level phosphorylation) when BPGA becomes 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA) and when phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) becomes pyruvic acid.

example.q: At which two steps is ATP used in glycolysis?
example.answer: In the two phosphorylation steps before the sugar splits.

learn.reallife: Sprinters at the Khelo India games rely heavily on glycolysis for quick bursts of energy before oxygen supply catches up.

quiz.q: How many enzyme-controlled reactions make up glycolysis?
quiz.explain: Glycolysis is a chain of ten reactions.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

A is true, but R is false

topics.title: Glycolysis: net yield and the fate of pyruvate

learn.hook: Glycolysis spends 2 ATP and makes 4. Like a shopkeeper's ledger, the net profit is what counts.
points: In plants, glucose comes from sucrose (the end product of photosynthesis) or from storage carbohydrates. Invertase converts sucrose into glucose and fructose, which both enter glycolysis.
ATP used: 2 (hexokinase step and fructose-6-P step). ATP made: 4 (two at BPGA → PGA and two at PEP → pyruvate, since each glucose gives two 3-carbon molecules). Net gain: 2 ATP.
Per glucose, glycolysis also gives 2 NADH + H⁺ and 2 molecules of pyruvic acid.
Pyruvic acid is the key product of glycolysis. Its fate depends on the cell's need.

Three fates: lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation (both anaerobic, in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes), and aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle, needs O₂) for complete oxidation to CO₂ and H₂O.

example.q: Calculate the net ATP from glycolysis of one glucose molecule.
steps: ATP formed: 2 at BPGA → PGA + 2 at PEP → pyruvate = 4.

learn.reallife: Sugarcane mills in Maharashtra ferment molasses (rich in sucrose) to ethanol for petrol blending under India's ethanol programme; the first step is splitting sucrose.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How much does glycolysis actually earn?' Do the ATP accounting and explain what happens to pyruvate!
teach.praise: Chirp! Spend 2, earn 4, net 2 ATP. Then pyruvate goes three possible ways!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the net ATP from glycolysis, and what are the fates of pyruvate?

learn.hook: Idli batter rises overnight and your legs ache after a long run. Both are fermentation stories.
points: Alcoholic fermentation (e.g. yeast): incomplete oxidation of glucose under anaerobic conditions; pyruvic acid is converted to CO₂ and ethanol by pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase.

Lactic acid fermentation: some bacteria convert pyruvic acid to lactic acid. In animal cells such as muscles during exercise, when O₂ is inadequate, pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase.
In both, NADH + H⁺ is reoxidised to NAD⁺, so glycolysis can continue.
Fermentation releases less than 7% of the energy in glucose, and not all of it is trapped as ATP. The net gain is only the 2 ATP of glycolysis.
The products are hazardous: acid or alcohol. Yeasts poison themselves to death when alcohol reaches about 13%.

example.q: Why does fermentation need to regenerate NAD⁺?
steps: Glycolysis uses NAD⁺ when PGAL is oxidised.
If NAD⁺ runs out, glycolysis stops.
Converting pyruvate to lactic acid or ethanol reoxidises NADH to NAD⁺.
example.answer: So glycolysis can continue and keep making ATP.

learn.reallife: Idli and dosa batters ferment with help from microbes that release CO₂, making them fluffy; curd forms by lactic acid fermentation.

topics.title: Aerobic respiration: link reaction and Krebs cycle

learn.hook: Hans Krebs worked out a cycle that turns one pyruvate into three CO₂ molecules and a stash of energy carriers. It runs nonstop in your mitochondria.
points: Aerobic respiration needs complete oxidation of pyruvate in mitochondria: stepwise removal of hydrogen leaving three CO₂ (in the matrix), and passing the electrons to O₂ with ATP synthesis (on the inner membrane).

Link reaction: in the matrix, pyruvate undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvic dehydrogenase (needing NAD⁺, coenzyme A and Mg²⁺): pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺. Two NADH form per glucose.
Krebs cycle (TCA cycle): acetyl group condenses with oxaloacetic acid (OAA) and water to form citric acid, catalysed by citrate synthase, releasing CoA. Citrate isomerises to isocitrate.

Two successive decarboxylations give α-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl CoA. Succinyl CoA → succinic acid makes one GTP (substrate-level phosphorylation), which gives ATP. The remaining steps regenerate OAA.
Per pyruvate in the cycle: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (via GTP). Including the link reaction: pyruvic acid + 4NAD⁺ + FAD⁺ + 2H₂O + ADP + Pi → 3CO₂ + 4NADH + 4H⁺ + FADH₂ + ATP.

example.q: How many NADH and FADH₂ are produced from one glucose in the link reaction plus Krebs cycle?
steps: Per pyruvate: 1 NADH (link) + 3 NADH (cycle) = 4 NADH, and 1 FADH₂.

learn.reallife: Endurance athletes, like marathoners at the Mumbai Marathon, depend heavily on aerobic respiration through the Krebs cycle in their muscle mitochondria.

topics.title: Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation

learn.hook: Cyanide is deadly because it blocks the last step of the electron transport chain. Without that step, oxygen can't do its job.
points: The electron transport system (ETS) is on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons from NADH are oxidised by NADH dehydrogenase (complex I) and passed to ubiquinone.

FADH₂ (from succinate oxidation) passes its reducing equivalents to ubiquinone via complex II. Reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) passes electrons to cytochrome c via the cytochrome bc₁ complex (complex III).

Cytochrome c is a small mobile protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane carrying electrons from complex III to complex IV. Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase, with cytochromes a and a₃ and two copper centres.
Oxygen is the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor, forming water. Its role is only at the terminal stage, but it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system.

Electron flow is coupled to ATP synthase (complex V: F₁ headpiece makes ATP; F₀ is the proton channel). Energy of oxidation-reduction builds a proton gradient (oxidative phosphorylation). 2H⁺ pass through F₀ from the intermembrane space to the matrix per ATP. One NADH gives 3 ATP; one FADH₂ gives 2 ATP.

example.q: How many ATP are produced by oxidising 4 NADH and 1 FADH₂ in the ETS?

learn.reallife: Cyanide poisoning cases treated in Indian hospitals are emergencies because cyanide stops complex IV, halting ATP production.

topics.title: The respiratory balance sheet: fermentation vs aerobic respiration

learn.hook: Aerobic respiration can yield up to 38 ATP per glucose; fermentation only 2. That's like comparing a full salary to pocket money.
points: Balance sheet assumptions: a sequential, orderly pathway (glycolysis → TCA → ETS); NADH from glycolysis enters mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation; no intermediates are withdrawn to make other compounds; only glucose is respired. These are not fully valid in real cells, where pathways run simultaneously.
Under these assumptions there is a net gain of 38 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration.
Count: glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH; link reaction 2 NADH; Krebs 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂. NADH total 10 × 3 = 30 ATP; FADH₂ 2 × 2 = 4 ATP; direct ATP 4. Total 38.
Fermentation vs aerobic: partial vs complete breakdown of glucose; net 2 ATP vs many more; NADH oxidised slowly vs vigorously.

Glycolysis vs Krebs: cytoplasm vs mitochondrial matrix; anaerobic vs needs O₂ (via ETS); glucose → 2 pyruvate vs acetyl CoA → CO₂. Respiration differs from combustion: it is stepwise, enzyme-controlled and traps energy as ATP rather than releasing it all as heat.

example.q: Use the balance sheet to verify 38 ATP per glucose.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways keeps an energy balance sheet for every train; cells keep one for every glucose molecule.

learn.hook: The respiratory pathway is not a one-way street to the dump yard. It's a busy junction where raw materials are also picked up to build new molecules.
points: Glucose is the favoured substrate, but others can be respired.
Fats are first broken into glycerol and fatty acids. Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA and enter the pathway; glycerol enters after conversion to PGAL.
Proteins are degraded by proteases; amino acids (after deamination) enter at various points: within the Krebs cycle, or as pyruvate or acetyl CoA.
The same intermediates are withdrawn when the organism needs to make fatty acids or proteins (e.g. acetyl CoA is withdrawn to make fatty acids).
Since the respiratory pathway is involved in both catabolism (breakdown) and anabolism (synthesis), it is better called an amphibolic pathway than a catabolic one.

example.q: Where do glycerol and fatty acids from a fat enter the respiratory pathway?
steps: Glycerol is converted to PGAL, an intermediate of glycolysis.
Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle.
example.answer: Glycerol enters as PGAL; fatty acids as acetyl CoA.

learn.reallife: Groundnut and mustard seeds, rich in oil, germinate by respiring stored fats through acetyl CoA, the same molecule they later use to build new fatty acids.

learn.hook: By measuring just two gases, CO₂ out and O₂ in, you can guess whether a seed is burning starch, oil or protein.
points: Respiratory quotient (RQ) = volume of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ consumed in respiration. It depends on the respiratory substrate.
Carbohydrates (completely oxidised): equal volumes of CO₂ and O₂, so RQ = 1. For glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O gives RQ = 6/6 = 1.
Fats: RQ is less than 1. Tripalmitin: 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O; RQ = 102/145 ≈ 0.7.
Proteins: RQ is about 0.9.
In living organisms, substrates are usually a mixture; pure proteins or fats are never used alone.

example.q: Calculate the RQ for malic acid: C₄H₆O₅ + 3O₂ → 4CO₂ + 3H₂O.

learn.reallife: Seed technologists at ICAR institutes use respirometers to study seed respiration; oil-rich mustard seeds show RQ below 1 while starchy wheat grains show about 1.

quiz.q: RQ is defined as:

options: Volume of O₂ consumed ÷ volume of CO₂ evolved
Volume of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ consumed

quiz.q: What is the RQ when glucose is completely oxidised?

quiz.q: The RQ of tripalmitin, 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O, is about:

quiz.q: For malic acid (C₄H₆O₅ + 3O₂ → 4CO₂ + 3H₂O), the RQ is:
quiz.explain: 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.33; organic acids give RQ above 1.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The RQ of carbohydrates is 1. Reason (R): Carbohydrates contain no oxygen atoms in their molecules.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: on complete oxidation, equal volumes of CO₂ are evolved and O₂ consumed, so RQ = 1. R is false: carbohydrates such as glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) are rich in oxygen.
quiz.mistake: Accepts the reason without checking it against the facts

teach.ask: Gappu measures gases from germinating seeds. Teach him how to calculate RQ and what it tells us about the substrate!
teach.praise: Chirp! CO₂ out divided by O₂ in: 1 for sugars, 0.7 for fats, 0.9 for proteins!
teach.nudge: Good! How is RQ calculated, and what is it for carbohydrates and fats?
